name: Italy
tagline: A country invented in 1861 out of places that still think of themselves first.
summary: Italy holds more UNESCO World Heritage sites than any other country and treats most of them as ordinary streets. It became one state only in 1861, and the food, dialect and civic pride still change every forty kilometres — the pasta shape tells you where you are. The Alps in the north are as serious as Switzerland's; the south is Greek, Arab and Norman by turns.

season.note: April to June and September to October. August is hot, and Italians themselves leave the cities for the coast, closing half the restaurants you wanted. The Dolomites have a separate July-September walking season and a December-March snow one.

getting_around: Frecciarossa and Italo make Milan–Rome three hours and compete on price. Regional trains are cheap and reach hill towns. Driving into historic centres is restricted by ZTL cameras and the fines arrive months later, abroad.
food: Pasta by region — trofie in Liguria, orecchiette in Puglia, carbonara only in Rome
Coffee standing at the bar, and never a cappuccino after breakfast
Wine by the region it is drunk in: Barolo north, Chianti centre, Etna south
know: Coperto is a per-person cover charge and is legal and normal; a tip on top is not expected.
ZTL zones in historic centres are camera-enforced — never drive in without a hotel permit.
Churches enforce covered shoulders and knees, including in high summer.

regions.name: Rome & Lazio
regions.summary: Three thousand years stacked vertically, and the hill towns and lakes around it.

cities.name: Rome
cities.summary: A city where an insurance office sits on a temple and nobody comments, with the best street-level food in Italy.
highlights: The Pantheon, entered free, still roofed by the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built
The Forum and Palatine early, before the heat and the groups
Testaccio market and the quinto quarto cooking around it
Borghese Gallery, two hours, booked, and worth restructuring a day for

experiences.name: Testaccio, where Rome eats
experiences.summary: The market and the streets around it are where Roman offal cooking survives; go at one, order what the sign says.

experiences.name: The Appian Way on a Sunday
experiences.summary: The road is closed to traffic on Sundays: basalt paving from 312 BC, catacombs, aqueducts and countryside, inside the city.

cities.name: Orvieto
cities.summary: A town on a plug of volcanic rock with a striped cathedral and an Etruscan city tunnelled underneath it.
highlights: The cathedral facade, and Signorelli's apocalypse frescoes inside
St Patrick's Well: a double-helix staircase 54 metres down
1,200 caves cut into the tufa beneath the streets

cities.name: Civita di Bagnoregio
cities.summary: A village on an eroding tufa pillar, reached by a footbridge, with about a dozen permanent residents left.
highlights: The bridge, which is the only way in and takes ten minutes
Etruscan tunnels cut under the rock
Watching the cliff edge, which loses a little every winter — the town is called 'the dying city' locally

regions.name: Tuscany & the Centre
regions.summary: The Renaissance where it happened, plus Siena's rivalry and the hill towns between.

cities.name: Florence
cities.summary: A banking city that funded the Renaissance and kept nearly all of it inside a twenty-minute walk.
highlights: Brunelleschi's dome, climbed at opening
The Uffizi, booked, and the Bargello, which is empty and holds the sculpture
San Miniato al Monte at vespers, with the monks singing
Bistecca alla fiorentina, which is a cut and a thickness, not a doneness

experiences.name: Vespers at San Miniato
experiences.summary: Gregorian chant in an 11th-century church above the city, at 17:30, free, and almost always uncrowded.

cities.name: Siena
cities.summary: A medieval city that lost to Florence and was preserved by losing, arranged around a shell-shaped square.
highlights: The Campo, and the Palio run around it twice each summer
The cathedral's inlaid marble floor, uncovered a few weeks a year
The contrade — seventeen districts with their own churches, museums and feuds

cities.name: Bologna
cities.summary: Forty kilometres of porticoes, the oldest university in the world, and the best eating in Italy.
highlights: The Quadrilatero's food shops, unchanged in layout since the Middle Ages
Portico di San Luca: 666 arches uphill to a basilica
Tagliatelle al ragù, which is what the world calls bolognese and is not the same thing

experiences.name: The 666 arches to San Luca
experiences.summary: Four kilometres of covered walkway climbing out of the city, built so a procession would never get wet.

cities.name: Lucca
cities.summary: An intact Renaissance wall, four kilometres round, wide enough on top to be a park, with a Roman amphitheatre turned into a square inside it.
highlights: Cycling the walls, which is what the whole city does at six
Piazza dell'Anfiteatro: the amphitheatre's oval, built over in houses
Puccini's birthplace, and concerts most evenings

experiences.name: Round the walls on a bicycle
experiences.summary: Four kilometres of Renaissance rampart, planted with plane trees in 1818 and used as a promenade ever since.

cities.name: Arezzo
cities.summary: A hill town with Piero della Francesca's greatest fresco cycle and none of Florence's queue.
highlights: The Legend of the True Cross in San Francesco, booked in slots of twenty-five
The sloping Piazza Grande, and the joust held on it twice a year
An antiques fair on the first weekend of every month

regions.name: The North & the Dolomites
regions.summary: Venice and its lagoon, Milan's money, the lakes, and limestone towers on the Austrian border.

cities.name: Venice
cities.summary: A city on wooden piles in a lagoon, with no roads, fewer than 50,000 residents left, and no equivalent anywhere.
highlights: Cannaregio and Castello, where people still live
The Accademia and the Punta della Dogana at opposite ends of taste
A traghetto across the Grand Canal, standing, for two euros
Torcello and the mosaics that predate the city

experiences.name: Cicchetti and an ombra
experiences.summary: Small plates and a small glass of wine at a bàcaro, standing, moving on after one — the Venetian version of an aperitivo.

cities.name: Ortisei & the Dolomites
cities.summary: Pale limestone towers over alpine meadows, in a valley where Ladin is still the first language.
highlights: Alpe di Siusi, the largest high-altitude meadow in Europe
Via ferrata routes built by soldiers in 1915–18
Rifugi serving South Tyrolean food at 2,000 metres

experiences.name: A night in a rifugio
experiences.summary: Dinner at seven, lights out at ten, and the Enrosadira — the pink glow on the rock at dawn — from the door.

cities.name: Milan
cities.summary: Italy's working city: fashion, design, finance, and a Last Supper that has to be booked months ahead.
highlights: The Duomo roof terraces, walked among the spires
Leonardo's Last Supper, fifteen minutes, booked in advance
Navigli canals at aperitivo hour

cities.name: Turin
cities.summary: The first capital of Italy: baroque arcades, an Egyptian museum second only to Cairo's, and vermouth invented in a bar here.
highlights: The Museo Egizio, which has more than most Egyptian cities
Eighteen kilometres of arcades, so the court could walk in the rain
Aperitivo, which Turin claims and Milan monetised

experiences.name: Vermouth where it was invented
experiences.summary: Carpano started here in 1786. The historic cafés still serve it the way it was drunk: cold, alone, with a small plate.

cities.name: Verona
cities.summary: A Roman arena still used for opera, a river bend of pink marble streets, and Valpolicella in the hills above.
highlights: Opera in the 1st-century arena, on cushions, in summer
San Zeno's bronze doors and Mantegna altarpiece
Amarone from Valpolicella, made from dried grapes

experiences.name: Opera in a Roman arena
experiences.summary: Fifteen thousand people, no amplification, and the cheap seats on the stone steps are the ones with the acoustics.

cities.name: Vernazza & the Cinque Terre
cities.summary: Five fishing villages on a cliff coast, joined by terraced footpaths and a railway in a tunnel.
highlights: The Sentiero Azzurro between villages, ticketed and sometimes closed by landslip
Dry-stone terraces holding the vineyards up — 6,700 km of wall in total
Anchovies from Monterosso, salted here for centuries

experiences.name: The terraces, from above
experiences.summary: The high paths behind the villages are free, empty and better; the coastal one is the queue.

cities.name: Bellagio & Lake Como
cities.summary: A village on the point where the lake divides, with villa gardens on both arms and ferries between them.
highlights: Villa Melzi and Villa Carlotta's gardens, best in May for the azaleas
The car ferry across to Varenna and Menaggio, used as transport
Walking up out of the villages into terraced chestnut woods

cities.name: Trieste
cities.summary: Austro-Hungarian, Italian, Slovene and Jewish at once, on a limestone edge above the Adriatic, with the best coffee culture in Italy.
highlights: Piazza Unità d'Italia, the largest sea-facing square in Europe
The Risiera di San Sabba, the only Nazi camp with a crematorium on Italian soil
Coffee ordered in a local dialect that confuses every other Italian

regions.name: Umbria & the Marches
regions.summary: The green middle: hill towns without Tuscany's traffic, a saint who changed the church, and the best-preserved Renaissance court in Italy.

cities.name: Assisi
cities.summary: A pink stone town on Monte Subasio, built around the basilica of a man who rejected everything it is made of.
highlights: Giotto's fresco cycle in the upper basilica, restored after the 1997 earthquake
The Eremo delle Carceri, the hermitage in the woods above town
Evening, when the day pilgrims leave and the town is a town

experiences.name: Up to the hermitage on foot
experiences.summary: An hour uphill through holm oak to the caves Francis actually used, which are quieter and more convincing than the basilica.

cities.name: Urbino
cities.summary: A hilltop ducal palace that was the model Renaissance court, in a town that has been a university since 1506.
highlights: Piero della Francesca's Flagellation, a small painting people travel for
The duke's studiolo, panelled in trompe-l'œil marquetry
Raphael's birthplace, on a steep street

regions.name: The South & the Islands
regions.summary: Naples, Pompeii, the Puglian heel, and Sicily's Greek temples under an active volcano.

cities.name: Naples
cities.summary: Loud, dense, Greek in origin, with the best pizza and the best archaeological museum in the world.
highlights: The Archaeological Museum, which holds everything good from Pompeii
Pizza in a room with a wood oven and four tables
Naples underground: Greek quarries, aqueducts and war shelters
Pompeii and Herculaneum, twenty minutes by local train

experiences.name: Fried pizza on the street
experiences.summary: Older and poorer than the baked kind, folded into a wallet and eaten walking; the sign to look for is a queue of locals.

cities.name: Matera
cities.summary: Cave dwellings inhabited for nine thousand years, evacuated in 1952 as a national disgrace, now a UNESCO site.
highlights: The Sassi, and rock churches with Byzantine frescoes
A restored cave house showing how families and animals shared one room
The gorge opposite, and the view back at night

cities.name: Palermo
cities.summary: Norman, Arab and Byzantine in the same building, with the best street food in Italy underneath.
highlights: The Cappella Palatina: Islamic ceiling, Byzantine mosaics, Norman king
Ballarò and Capo markets, shouted rather than sold
Monreale's mosaics, twenty minutes uphill

experiences.name: Palermo by street food
experiences.summary: Panelle, arancine, sfincione, and — if you are brave — pani ca meusa. A thousand years of occupation in six snacks.

cities.name: Syracuse & Ortigia
cities.summary: Once the most powerful Greek city in the world, now an island old town with a Doric temple inside the cathedral.
highlights: The cathedral, built inside a 5th-century BC temple, columns and all
The Greek theatre, still used for classical drama each summer
Swimming off the rocks at the tip of Ortigia at sunset

cities.name: Lecce
cities.summary: Baroque carved in soft golden limestone, in the heel of Italy, an hour from two seas.
highlights: Santa Croce's facade, which took a century and shows it
A Roman amphitheatre found under the main square in 1901
Orecchiette, and the Salento coast on both sides

cities.name: Alghero, Sardinia
cities.summary: A Catalan-speaking walled port on Sardinia's northwest coast, with sea caves and Bronze Age towers inland.
highlights: Catalan street signs, and a dialect spoken since the 14th century
Neptune's Grotto, reached by 654 steps down a cliff
Nuraghi: 7,000 stone towers across the island, from 1800 BC

experiences.name: Inside a nuraghe
experiences.summary: Su Nuraxi at Barumini is the UNESCO one, but there are seven thousand of these dry-stone towers and you can walk into many of them alone.

cities.name: Lipari & the Aeolians
cities.summary: Seven volcanic islands off Sicily, one of them erupting every twenty minutes, all of them on the UNESCO list.
highlights: Stromboli's explosions, watched from a boat at dusk
Pumice and obsidian quarries on Lipari, white against black
Hydrofoils between islands as ordinary transport

experiences.name: Stromboli, from the water
experiences.summary: The volcano has erupted more or less continuously for two thousand years. Boats hold position off the Sciara del Fuoco after dark.
